title: Projects
section: Project 3: Noble House & NPC Relationship Map for D&D
text:
Project 3: Noble House & NPC Relationship Map for D&D
In one of my classes, we worked with a well-known dataset: the noble houses of Renaissance Florence and the marriages that connected them. The D&D campaign I’ve been running draws heavily on that same period, and the overlap was hard to ignore — it seemed like a natural excuse to practice social network analysis on something I actually cared about. I built the first version of this project as a Quarto document over winter break, and that’s also when I first got excited about the tidygraph and visNetwork ecosystem in R.
Around the same time, I’d been hoping to bring ERGMs — a statistical modeling approach for networks — into some of my other coursework and projects. That didn’t pan out: statnet, the package that actually runs them, doesn’t work well with tidygraph/igraph objects, and that disappointment ended up bleeding into my enthusiasm here too, since it was riding the same wave of excitement. This project also had its own separate barrier — building out enough houses and NPCs by hand to make the graph worth looking at required a lot of tedious world-building before there was anything interesting to see. Between the two, momentum stalled out over the winter.
What got it moving again was converting the whole thing into a Shiny app, with random name and seed-data generation built in — which solved the world-building barrier directly, and finally made this something worth showing to friends or anyone curious enough to build their own noble house drama.
The Florentine network we studied in class only modeled relationships between the houses themselves. I wanted to go further: a two-mode network that also captures the NPCs, the relationships between individuals, and the ties connecting people to the institutions that shape their lives.
A lot of this could also be handled in Obsidian, which I’m a big proponent of — but the lessons learned and the fun of building it were worth the detour on their own.
Next up: easier ways to bring in existing tables for personality traits, bonds, and flaws, plus homebrew rolling tables for house-level attributes like wealth and industry.


What it does - Add houses and NPCs, wire up relationships between them - Relationship types auto-filter based on what’s actually valid between the two entities you pick - Edit, delete, and reorganize as the campaign evolves
Built with: R, Shiny, tidygraph/igraph, visNetwork, bslib

title: About Me
text:
I believe those who advance the bounds of knowledge bear responsibility for the direction of that work and what it’s used for. Applying the sociological imagination to real-world data problems means looking past what methods are used to why they were chosen, and what that choice implies about the resulting data. As a graduate student in computational social science, I use NLP and social network analysis to understand how information, influence, and power move through real-world systems. I hope to put that work toward data for good — using these tools to make positive and meaningful impacts on the world.

title: Projects
text:
Mask R-CNN redaction detection — each red box is a model-detected redaction, annotated with its confidence score.







The 100 highest-degree nodes in the pooled communication network.





The Department of Justice’s release of the Epstein email records offers a rare chance to observe an elite communication network directly rather than through court testimony or journalistic reconstruction. With two collaborators, I built a Python pipeline that extracts headers from roughly 1.4 million released email records — classifying pages with dual OCR engines, locating redactions with a fine-tuned Mask R-CNN, and recovering sender and recipient fields — then resolved names in R through a six-pass matching pipeline into a longitudinal directed network of 990 confirmed individuals across 21 yearly waves (2000–2020), totaling 6,250 unique communication ties.
The network is modeled with Bootstrapped Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models (BTERGM) to test two hypotheses drawn from the literature on brokerage and gendered social capital:

H1: Actors in structural brokerage positions (low lagged Burt’s constraint) are disproportionately active in tie formation.
H2: Ties form disproportionately between individuals of the same sex.

Both hypotheses are supported. Low-constraint brokers are significantly more likely to send and receive ties, and same-sex dyads are 15.7% more likely to form than mixed-sex dyads, net of reciprocity, transitivity, and tie persistence. A secondary finding shows an asymmetric sex pattern: women are significantly more likely to initiate ties, while men are significantly more likely to receive them — women disproportionately write, men are disproportionately written to. A follow-up beta regression on Burt’s constraint (restricted to nodes with actual brokerage opportunity) finds women occupy significantly more broker-like positions than men, net of year fixed effects.
A time series extension separately models monthly redaction density with auto.arima(). The aggregate series shows a clear upward drift trend — which disappears when emails not directly involving Epstein are modeled alone, suggesting the drift tracks his centrality specifically rather than a general feature of the corpus. Redaction density also carries a stable gender pattern: F→F communications are the most heavily redacted, concentrated almost entirely among non-Epstein actors.
This work was completed in collaboration with Mark Scott and Elizabeth Miller, and won Best Master’s Project at the computational social science fair.
Data visualizations & full results · GitHub

title: Data Visualizations
text:
This page walks through the visual and statistical results from a few of my ongoing projects.

Epstein Email NetworkPolitical Podcast Text Analysis


For the full modeling code and diagnostics, see the project write-up or get in touch via the Contact page.

Redaction Detection Pipeline
Before any network could be built, every one of the ~1.4 million released pages had to be run through a fine-tuned Mask R-CNN model to locate redactions, paired with dual OCR engines to recover the surrounding text.



Mask R-CNN redaction detection on a sample email. Each red box is a model-detected redaction; the small numbers above each box are the model’s confidence score.





The Aggregated Network



987 non-isolate nodes, 21 yearly waves pooled. All identities are intentionally suppressed — the analysis concerns network structure, not the identification of individuals.


The pooled network shows the classic core–periphery shape of an ego-anchored corpus: a dense communicative core surrounded by hundreds of low-degree contacts extending outward in long chains.


Growth Over Time






Network activity by year — unique dyads, senders, and receivers.







Network density by year.





Activity is sparse before Epstein’s 2008 plea agreement and climbs steadily afterward, motivating the decision to estimate the final model on the 2009–2019 window rather than the full 2000–2020 panel.


Who Emails Whom?



Share of each sender group’s ties, by recipient sex.


A first descriptive look at same-sex clustering: male senders direct 70% of their ties to other men, while female senders direct 63% of theirs to men — women’s outgoing ties are noticeably less sex-segregated than men’s. This descriptive pattern alone can’t separate real homophily from confounds like reciprocity or degree heterogeneity, which is exactly what the temporal ERGM below is built to isolate.


Temporal ERGM Results



TERGM final model — 20 time steps. Bootstrap 95% CIs (R = 1,000); asterisk marks CIs that exclude zero.





Odds ratios, visualized (2009–2019 window).


Both hypotheses are supported, net of reciprocity, tie persistence, transitivity, and degree distribution:

Brokerage (H1): Low-constraint brokers are significantly more active senders and receivers (Sender constraint OR = 0.28; Receiver constraint OR = 0.26).
Homophily (H2): Same-sex ties are 15.7% more likely to form than mixed-sex ties (OR = 1.16).

The sex main effects reveal an asymmetry beyond the homophily result: male senders are significantly less likely to initiate ties (OR = 0.75), while male receivers are significantly more likely to receive them (OR = 1.16) — women disproportionately write, men are disproportionately written to.

Goodness of Fit



ROC and Precision-Recall curves for the final model.


Out-of-sample tie prediction is strong, though a substantial share of that performance is carried by the memory (tie-persistence) term — persistence, not novelty, dominates elite email networks.



Brokerage and Sex



Lagged Burt’s constraint by sex, active node-years 2009–2019. Lower values indicate more broker-like positioning; dashed lines mark group means.


The supplementary question behind H1: who actually occupies the brokerage positions the model rewards? Burt’s constraint is bimodal — most people cluster near full constraint (1.0, no brokerage opportunity), with a smaller broker-like cluster near 0.5.



Brokerage model — beta regression, restricted to active nodes with non-maximal constraint (excluding nodes with no brokerage opportunity).


Restricting to nodes with actual brokerage opportunity (constraint < 1) and controlling for year fixed effects, the sex gap is statistically significant (β = 0.160, 95% CI [0.057, 0.263], z = 3.05, N = 1,482): women disproportionately occupy the broker-like positions in this network, net of temporal trends.


Most Active Members






Top nodes by total degree.







Top 100 nodes by degree — 67 male, 33 female.







Interpretation
Existing research on sex trafficking networks identifies a specific advantage women hold within them: an ability to connect with, and gain the trust of, other women. Under patriarchy, women are disproportionately the targets of violence — sexual and otherwise — most often at the hands of men, frequently men they already know. That shared experience of vulnerability creates a baseline of trust between women that trafficking networks can and do exploit. Women recruiting women isn’t incidental; it’s a structural feature of how these networks operate.
None of this means patriarchy is really about gender. It’s about power — who holds it, and who it can be directed against. Gender is simply the axis along which that power most often gets organized and legitimized; the same logic of domination shows up across other hierarchies too.
The results above are consistent with that framing. Women in this network were significantly more likely to initiate contact and occupied a modest but statistically significant brokerage advantage over men — exactly the pattern the trafficking-network literature predicts: women doing more of the connective, trust-dependent work, while remaining structurally subordinate within the network’s power hierarchy.


Time Series Extension
A separate analysis models monthly email volume and redaction density as time series (auto.arima()), and disaggregates redaction density by gender dyad and by Epstein’s direct involvement.
Temporal baseline: the aggregate redaction density series requires a drift term to fit — ARIMA(1,1,1) with drift, confirming a systematic upward trend across 2010–2019. That drift disappears entirely in the subset of emails not directly involving Epstein — ARIMA(0,1,1), no drift — suggesting the upward trend is concentrated in Epstein-involved correspondence rather than being network-wide.



Monthly redaction density by gender dyad, 2010–2019.


Gender dyad pattern: redaction density carries a stable ordering across the full period — F→F highest, then F→M, M→F, M→M lowest. This ordering holds across temporal resolutions and the full dataset.



Monthly redaction density by gender dyad, faceted by Epstein involvement.


Disaggregating by Epstein involvement shows where this pattern actually lives. In the From Epstein panel, all four dyads cluster low with no meaningful gender ordering — Epstein’s own outgoing emails are uniformly lightly redacted regardless of recipient sex. The To Epstein panel shows modest differentiation but no strong trend. The gender effect is concentrated almost entirely in the No Epstein panel, where F→F and F→M redaction density rise steadily and diverge from the male-sender dyads — suggesting this is a property of the broader network, not of Epstein’s direct correspondence.
Read together with the network results: women were significantly more likely to initiate ties, occupied a significant (if modest) brokerage advantage, and their communications — particularly with other women — were the most heavily redacted in the corpus. Women’s roles in this network were both structurally central and disproportionately sensitive.
Limitations: gender assignment relied on fuzzy matching and probabilistic inference, and some names were dropped where assignment failed. Redaction density is a proxy — the underlying redaction decisions, legal framework, and any changes to FOIA processing standards over the period aren’t observable from the data. The gender dyad and Epstein-involvement breakdowns above are descriptive; no formal interaction model (e.g. mixed effects, interrupted time series) has yet tested these differences directly.
